title: Migration lanes from vLLM/TGI to managed inference: decision heuristics & GTM hooks
body:
Executive summary:

This note provides practical migration lanes and concise decision heuristics for engineering and product teams considering a shift from self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM variants) to a managed Redwood inference offering. Focus: when to recommend build vs buy, what ops risks to emphasize to buyers, and prescriptive GTM hooks for pilot->enterprise motion.

Why this matters (framing for sales):
- Many teams start with open-source runtimes to iterate quickly, but latent operational complexity (cost surprises, tail latency, model maintenance) becomes a salesable problem as usage grows.
- Our goal: give field reps a crisp narrative that maps technical pain to Redwood value (predictable unit economics, SLA-backed latency, rollout controls, private options for compliance).

Migration lanes (practical paths we see in the field):
1) Rapid flip (POC -> managed within 4–8 weeks)
   - Typical customer: product team with a prototype on vLLM/TGI, low token volumes (<200M tokens/month), velocity to market matters, limited SRE headcount.
   - Risk drivers: operational overhead, infra debt, bursty traffic causing throttling.
   - Redwood hook: quick onboarding, same API semantics, fast switch with traffic split, predictable cost forecast.
   - Success criteria: latency parity within 10–20% for common prompt lengths, no production incidents during 30-day pilot.

2) Hybrid scaling lane (gradual migration + Dedicated for hotspots)
   - Typical customer: product with production traffic trending to >1B tokens/month, mix of latency-sensitive features and background batch jobs.
   - Risk drivers: autoscaling complexity, effective batching strategies, cold-start/eviction churn across model variants.
   - Redwood hook: Dedicated pools for stable SLOs, autoscaling policies tuned to SLOs, prefix/KV caching to preserve latency at scale.
   - Success criteria: 30–40% reduction in token-unit cost after tuning, stable p99 latency under load tests.

3) Regulated/private lane (on-prem/VPC + compliance)
   - Typical customer: finance/healthcare/legal with strict data residency/security needs, often require HSM/KMS and audit evidence.
   - Risk drivers: deploying hardened runtimes in air-gapped or VPC environments, restricted kernel support for quantized models.
   - Redwood hook: Private deployment with compliance integrations, enterprise rollouts and support playbooks.
   - Success criteria: successful STIG-like checklist signoff, audit logs enabled, and DR runbook validated.

Technical delta (prose comparison, for quick field reference):
- vLLM / TGI / open runtimes: fast iteration, good community momentum, but often single-node optimizations, limited multi-tenant telemetry, manual batching, and fragile autoscaling. TensorRT-LLM: excellent inference speed for certain hardware/quantizations but high engineering integration costs and vendor lock-in nuances.
- Redwood managed: production-grade batching + KV caching, dynamic kernel selection across HW types, integrated tracing and token-level cost attribution, autoscaling policies tuned for latency SLOs, SLA guarantees, and built-in fallback routing.
- Net effect: open runtimes win early TTM; managed wins at scale (economic predictability, fewer incidents, easier rollouts).

Decision heuristics (simple rules reps can use):
1) Tokens/day threshold: consider buy when sustained token volume > ~500M/month OR when month-over-month growth > 20% and engineering headcount cannot scale proportionally.
2) SLO sensitivity: buy if p99 latency requirements are strict (<300ms for short prompts) or if bursty traffic must not degrade user experience.
3) Compliance bar: buy if data cannot leave customer network or audits require detailed operator logs—trigger Private/Dedicated sales path.
4) Feature velocity vs ops headcount: buy if the product roadmap requires shipping model changes every 2–4 weeks but SRE headcount < 2.

GTM hooks and messaging snippets (for quick use):
- For engineering leads: "Keep the iteration speed of open-source for experiments, and offload the production uncertainty to a partner who treats inference like a distributed database—predictable, observable, and SLA-backed."
- For platform/SRE: "Replace firefighting cycles with control plane tooling: token-level cost insights, per-route dashboards, and safe rollouts—so you can enforce capacity policies by team."
- For procurement/security: "Private deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; we provide a clear handoff for security signoff and a single vendor for SLAs and support."

Pricing and contracting levers to surface early:
- Commit tiers (monthly tokens) to reduce unit price and justify Dedicated pool sizing.
- Pilot credits for the first 30–60 days to demonstrate latency and cost benefits with no upfront infra spend.
- Migration credits: offset part of the integration work (ingestion adapters, auth shims) for enterprise customers moving from on-prem stacks.

Common objections & short counters:
- "We already have vLLM and infra — we can scale it ourselves."
  Counter: "Scaling code is one thing; scaling reliably under unknown model and usage distributions is different. We’ve seen predictable patterns where ops cost scales faster than token cost savings after 6–9 months—our benchmarks show predictable unit economics and fewer on-call incidents."
- "We need custom kernel optimizations (TensorRT) for cost parity."
  Counter: "TensorRT wins for very specific matrix sizes and quant setups. Redwood’s runtime supports similar kernel selection and we’ll co-run benchmarks during pilot; in Dedicated/private cases we can also support vendor-specific optimizations and advise on model quantization tradeoffs."
- "Data residency prevents managed services."
  Counter: "Private deployments and VPC options are specifically designed for these cases; we’ll map the audit requirements to controls we can provide or support in an on-prem package."

Pilot structure (recommended 6–8 week plan):
1) Week 0: Kickoff, define success metrics (latency, cost per 1k tokens, error rate).
2) Week 1–2: Baseline collection on current self-hosted stack (synthetic + production traces anonymized).
3) Week 3–4: Deploy equivalent model variant on Redwood, run traffic split 10/90, validate results.
4) Week 5: Tune batching/quantization policies and autoscaling; collect cost telemetry.
5) Week 6–8: Ramp to 50–100% with rollback guardrails; finalize migration runbook and run DR test.

Operational playbook highlights to reassure technical buyers:
- Observability: token-level cost and latency breakdowns, model-version traces, and per-route dashboards to isolate regression causes.
- Rollouts: canary with automatic fallback to previous model variant and cross-region routing to handle capacity events.
- Incident response: SRE playbooks pre-baked for OOM, degraded quantized kernels, and GPU driver incompatibilities; runbook shared during pilot.

Signals that justify a second meeting with engineering (and what to bring):
- They have production traffic patterns (traffic matrix, p95/p99 latencies) and a backlog of production incidents tied to inference.
- They are unable to forecast monthly unit costs because of autoscaling unpredictability.
- They need audit artifacts or need to move to VPC/on-prem in next 6 months.

Appendix: quick technical checklist (for field engineers to validate during discovery)
- Current stack: vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM? model size, token distribution, prompt length percentiles.
- Hardware: GPU types, memory per GPU, NVMe config, interconnect (RDMA?)
- Quantization state: fp16/int8/4-bit? and any custom kernels in place.
- Autoscaling: how is capacity provisioned? manual scale, HPA, custom controllers?
- Observability: what telemetry exists (token-level traces, batch sizes, cache hit rates)?

Sample outreach email (engineering-friendly):
"Hey <Name>,

We’ve helped teams that started on vLLM/TGI move to a managed inference model while keeping iteration velocity. A short pilot can show whether you get predictable latency and a clear cost profile without re-architecting your product. Can we run a 6-week benchmark with your top-producing model and show a direct comparison?

Cheers,
Ravi Patel — Redwood Inference"

Closing notes:
- Keep the message empathetic: building is not a mistake—it's the right choice early. The field story that resonates is: "You can keep building, but don’t buy the operational risk you don’t need."
- Focus pilots on measurable wins (cost per 1K tokens, p99 latency improvement, reduction in incidents) and use those metrics to convert platform and exec stakeholders.

Unresolved questions to follow up with product/engineering:
- Can we produce a standardized benchmark package (scripts + synthetic workload generator) that covers common prompt-length distributions to make pilot setup < 48 hours?
- What are guardrails for supporting customers that insist on low-level kernel mods (how do we support or dissuade without promising bespoke work)?

(End of note)
